introduction: The word these passages turn on is ḥikmat, wisdom, and in Bahá’u’lláh’s tablets it most often means something practical: knowing what to say, to whom, when, and how much. It is a counsel given to a persecuted community, some of whose members had brought disaster on themselves and others by speaking rashly, and it widens into a whole ethic of speech, consultation, caution, patience and trust that what is not understood has a reason. A hundred of the guide’s three hundred quotations are given here, drawn in proportion from its eight sections. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: Proverbs above all, James on the tongue, Paul on milk and meat, the Qur’an on verifying a report, Confucius, Aristotle, Polonius, Pope, Bacon. About one in five presses from the other side and ends in a question: Jesus on the housetops and on denying him before men, Peter before the council, Daniel at his open window, Emerson and Milton on plain speech, Kant on who decides what a person may hear, Machiavelli and Falstaff on what else goes by the name of prudence, and Ivan Karamazov on hidden wisdom.
questions: “Not everything that a man knoweth can be disclosed.” Kant thought it immaturity to let another decide what one may know. Who is entitled to judge a hearer’s capacity, and how would you want it judged in your own case?
The friends are told to leave a veil, avoid tumult and keep silent before governments; the apostles said, “We cannot but speak.” What distinguishes the wisdom asked for here from fear?
Bahá’u’lláh mocks a “wisdom” that only preserves the self, and Falstaff calls discretion the better part of valour. How do you tell prudence from self-protection in a decision you have had to make?
Believers were permitted to conceal their faith under threat of death, and Jesus warns against denying him before men. Where is the line between concealment and denial?
Gentle words, measured to the hearer, are praised throughout; Emerson wants hard words and Milton an open contest. When has gentleness served the truth in your experience, and when has it blunted it?
“Everything which happens is due to some wisdom.” Ivan Karamazov returns his ticket. When, and to whom, is it right to say that a calamity has a hidden reason?

outside.why: If the veil is torn away, “none will draw near to hear the word of truth”. Confucius: when a man may not be spoken with, to speak to him is to err in reference to our words. The wise err neither in regard to their man nor to their words.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that a delicate veil be left. Jesus told the twelve: what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops. When is discretion wisdom, and when is it a way of not saying what must be said?
“A kindly tongue is the lodestone of the hearts of men.” Proverbs: a soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
The knower should explain, and “the listener can decide for themselves”. Pope’s rule for giving advice: men must be taught as if you taught them not.
“Don’t try to force these opinions upon the people … The kingdom is one of good pleasure, not of force.” The Qur’an: there is no compulsion in religion.
“Man has two ears and one tongue, so he should hear twice and speak once.” James: let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak.
Not the wisdom that keeps silent, but one of “tolerance, love, kindness, patience”. James: the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated.
Utterance has influence only from “hearts which are detached and pure”. Paul: my speech was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit.
“Utterance must needs possess penetrating power.” Hebrews: the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword.
Utterance needs moderation, or “the hearer would be unable to bear it”. Aristotle on the hard part of any virtue: to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, in the right way.
“One word may be likened unto fire, another unto light.” Proverbs: death and life are in the power of the tongue.
The wise should “speak with words as mild as milk”. Paul: I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it.
“One word is like unto fire that consumeth.” James: the tongue is a fire; behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
“A harsh word is even as a sword thrust; a gentle word as milk.” Proverbs: there is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.

Bahá’u’lláh asks for gentle words, measured to the hearer. Emerson: speak what you think now in hard words, and tomorrow speak what tomorrow thinks in hard words again. What does each fear will be lost?
“Utterance must needs be proportioned to the capacity of each soul.” Mark on Jesus: he spake the word unto them, as they were able to hear it.
“People are like earth — some barren, some blessed.” Jesus’ sower, whose seed falls by the wayside, on stony places, among thorns, and on good ground.
Where no good soil is found, “silence is preferable”. Jesus: neither cast ye your pearls before swine.
“Not everything that a man knoweth can be disclosed, nor … regarded as timely.” Jesus to his disciples: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
Much is to be withheld until the hearer is ready. Kant thought it the mark of immaturity to wait for a guardian to decide what one may know. Who decides when a person is ready, and by what right?
Some “give meat instead of milk to the infant”. Hebrews: strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age.
“Open … the city of the human heart with the key of your utterance.” Proverbs: by long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone.
The Cause is to be taught “through the power of men’s utterance, and not through resort to” force. Paul: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal.

“Sow not … the seeds of dissension … Be patient under all conditions.” Paul to Timothy: be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort. How does one tell patience from the failure to speak?
“Of all the gifts of God the greatest is the gift of Teaching … our first obligation.” Paul: necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
“The heaven of divine wisdom is illumined with two luminaries: consultation and compassion.” Proverbs: in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
“Every matter must be carried out through consultation.” The Qur’an praises those whose affairs are a matter of counsel.
Do not “accept claims from any soul merely on the basis of assertion”. The Qur’an: if an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance.
“Trust not every speaker, reveal not what thou knowest to every visitor.” Polonius to his son: give every man thy ear, but few thy voice.
Do not “believe every speaker, nor trust every claimant”. John’s letter: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.
“Trust not every newcomer.” Proverbs: the simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.

“Most of the souls in the world appear with deceit and guile, therefore wisdom must be observed.” Jesus: I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Most people, says the tablet, come with deceit. Paul’s charity “believeth all things, hopeth all things”. How does a person stay wary and still think well of others?
Investigation of others’ wrongs is necessary “within limits”, not as an occupation. Jesus: why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye?
“A wise person … never wastes time, saying ‘time is a cutting sword.’” Paul: walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time.
A caravan crossing dangerous country “must certainly be mindful of its protection”. Proverbs: a prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself.
“During the season of seed-sowing you cannot gather a crop.” The Preacher: a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted.
This is the season for sowing, not harvesting. Jesus: one soweth, and another reapeth.

“How many meanings are there that words cannot contain!” and how many whose time has not come. The Tao Te Ching: he who knows does not speak; he who speaks does not know. Is the silence in the meaning, or in the hour?
God has forgiven all; “they too must occupy themselves with reconciliation and forgive one another”. Jesus: first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
“The harm of discord is greater than the benefit of wisdom.” Paul: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not.
“Although he thought he was acting according to wisdom, he was mistaken.” Pope: fools rush in where angels fear to tread.

Believers who are lax in some observance “should not be dealt with harshly”; what is not yet possible is not demanded. Paul: if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth.
If even a favoured person acts against wisdom, “following him is not … permissible”. Jesus: if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
“Discord is a consuming fire that must be quenched by the waters of wisdom and utterance.” The Preacher: the words of wise men are heard in quiet more than the cry of him that ruleth among fools.
Strive “to remove differences that arise between the friends”. Jesus: blessed are the peacemakers.
“Let counsel be written to him — if he improves his character, better; if not, afterward …” Jesus gives the same order of steps: tell him his fault between thee and him alone.
A religious leader rises in malice: “work to calm his flame, show patience and forbearance”. Paul: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
“Be ye prudent, be ye discreet”, for the enemy lies in wait. Amos: the prudent shall keep silence in that time; for it is an evil time.
The friends are told not to rend the veil while enemies watch. Peter and John, forbidden to teach: we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard. Were they imprudent?

Bahá’u’lláh scorns the “wisdom” that only preserves the self: a drop of love would burn a hundred thousand prudences. Falstaff, rising from pretended death: the better part of valour is discretion. How does one tell prudence from Falstaff’s kind?
Love casts prudence to the wind. The Song of Solomon: many waters cannot quench love; if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.
Two things are desired: “wisdom and utterance, and … steadfastness”. Joshua: be strong and of a good courage.
“Show forth that which will ensure the peace and the well-being of the miserable and the downtrodden.” Proverbs: open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.
People imagine the friends “engaged in unseemly words and cursing and reviling prominent persons”. The Qur’an forbids even reviling false gods, lest God be reviled in return.
“Until ye find an ear, open not your lips.” Proverbs: a word spoken in due season, how good is it!

Some raised a clamour by speaking without wisdom. Milton wanted truth in the field at all costs: let her and Falsehood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worse in a free and open encounter? Is a clamour always a sign that something went wrong?
“In their vain imaginings they have increased their ignorant zeal and useless prejudices.” Paul: they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
“Any matter that causeth tumult among the people is assuredly contrary to wisdom.” Paul: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Tumult is to be avoided. The first Christians were accused of having turned the world upside down. Can a new teaching be brought without it?
Many “have acted without wisdom, thereby causing … the outcry of the deniers”. Jesus: which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?
“Due to the absence of hearing faculties, silence is preferable.” The Preacher: a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
“If it is accepted, the purpose is achieved; if not, contention is vain.” Jesus: whosoever shall not receive you, shake off the dust of your feet.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes this verse: “Fain would they put out God’s light with their mouths.”
If a thing can be sent so that none become aware, “it is beloved; otherwise, some delay is preferable”. John: then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret.
“Every secret that passeth beyond two will be divulged.” Proverbs: he that hath knowledge spareth his words.
Travelling teachers should not “stay openly in the home of a well-known believer”. Jesus: when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another.

What is commanded, “if not in accord with wisdom, should be held in abeyance” until the clamour dies. Daniel, when prayer was made a crime, prayed at his open window as he did aforetime. When is it right to suspend an observance, and when to keep it in the open?
In Shíráz he should first “seek out the company of the eminent” and win them by his conduct. Paul: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.
The announcement “should be given forth with wisdom, and not in haste”. Paul at Athens began from an altar his hearers had built themselves.
“Do not distress them by saying that they should not have done this or that. They will see by themselves.” Jesus: no man having drunk old wine straightway desireth new.
In Shíráz, “strangers may never become aware”. Joseph of Arimathaea: a disciple of Jesus, but secretly.

In wartime it is impossible to make the Cause a public spectacle: “all peoples and nations are occupied with bloodshed”. Mark Twain wrote, and did not publish in his lifetime, what a congregation at war could not bear to hear.
“Do not, for the time being, call that site by this name.” Esther in the king’s house: she had not shewed her people nor her kindred.
“My highest longing is to keep this fast, but wisdom must be considered.” Isaiah’s God prefers one kind of fast to another. What can rightly outweigh an observance one longs to keep?
After the martyrs, “the command of wisdom was revealed” in place of dissimulation. The Qur’an had excused one who is forced to deny while his heart is still content with faith.
Believers are told to be discreet about their faith for the sake of their lives. Jesus: whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny. Where does discretion end and denial begin?
Mention it to the governor only when it can be done fittingly. Jesus, asked a question meant to trap him with the authorities.

All are commanded to “wisdom and love”, so that even a consul is pleased. Machiavelli’s prudence allows a prince to break faith when it suits him. What makes the wisdom of these tablets a different thing from policy?

If living in the house “would cause clamor … residence therein is not permitted”. Naaman asks pardon in advance for bowing in his master’s temple, and Elisha says only: go in peace. How much accommodation does peace with one’s neighbours justify?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes this verse: “a believing man from among Pharaoh’s people who concealed his faith”.
“Wisdom does not require this now — the time will come.” The Preacher: in the morning sow thy seed, for thou knowest not whether shall prosper.
A House of Worship may be built “with the utmost discretion”, among trusted friends. Jesus: when thou prayest, enter into thy closet.
“Speak not a word that would cause the people around thee to flee.” Paul: let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt.

“It is not permissible to mention the Cause before the government.” Peter before the council: we ought to obey God rather than men. How do the readings square obedience to God with caution before rulers?
Vivisection should be confined, and done with “the greatest degree of carefulness”, the animal made insensible. Proverbs: a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast.
“We ask for things which the divine wisdom does not desire for us.” Shakespeare: we, ignorant of ourselves, beg often our own harms, which the wise powers deny us for our good.
There is no answer to such a prayer. Jesus to two disciples who asked for the best seats: ye know not what ye ask.

“Everything which happens is due to some wisdom … Therein is a mystery.” Ivan Karamazov will not have a harmony bought with a child’s tears, and returns his ticket. What can be said to him that is not an insult to the grief?
Conditional fate can be avoided; “it is expedient … to be cautious and prudent”. Aesop’s Hercules to the man with the cart in the mud: put your shoulder to the wheel.
“In the occurrence of this calamity a profound wisdom is hidden.” Joseph to the brothers who sold him: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.
“In every one of Thy deeds there is wisdom upon wisdom, and mystery upon mystery.” Paul: how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
“You will witness the wisdom behind your lack of success in the previous year.” Jesus to Peter: what I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter.
Disasters are “hard to bear yet inwardly there lies a great wisdom”. The Qur’an: it may happen that ye hate a thing which is good for you.

Behind cataclysms lies a wisdom that will appear later. Voltaire, after the Lisbon earthquake: you would compose a general bliss from individuals’ woes? When is it right to speak of hidden wisdom, and to whom?
Whatever comes into being is “according to the requirements of divine wisdom”. Julian of Norwich was told: it behoved that there should be sin; but all shall be well.
“In all that we have borne there lies hidden a wisdom that none knoweth save God.” Moses’ guide in the Qur’an warns him: how canst thou bear with that whereof thou canst not compass any knowledge?
Were the mysteries of God’s wisdom unravelled, enemies would be confounded. Job was answered with a question: where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?
Teachers are scarce who “observe wisdom, and … speak with such eloquence as to influence” the heart. Bacon: discretion of speech is more than eloquence.
“The sore athirst are many but the cup-bearers are few.” Jesus: the harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few.
